screens.title: Secure Smart Contract Development Practices
screens.subtitle: Design, code, and log defensively to reduce attack surface and operational risk

narration.text: In this chapter we move from knowing common vulnerabilities to building contracts that resist them. You will learn patterns and practical checks that make reentrancy, integer manipulation, and privilege escalation far less likely. We focus on mental models you carry into every function: validate inputs, update state, and only then call externally; prefer language-level arithmetic safety when available; and centralize access checks into reusable modifiers. You will also learn how to handle external calls safely, design for gas, and emit events so off-chain monitors can audit behavior. These practices matter because smart contracts are immutable once deployed; small mistakes lead to costly breaches or irreversible failures. As a concrete use case, we will refactor a vulnerable token contract to use Solidity 0.8.0 safety features, add explicit ownership checks, apply the Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern to withdrawals, and emit events for observability. By the end, you should be able to read a function and say whether it follows CEI, whether arithmetic is safe, and whether access is enforced. Consider this a shift: from reactive patching to proactive engineering. How would you change your default development checklist after this chapter?

keyIdea.title: Chapter focus
keyIdea.text: Adopt secure defaults: validate inputs, update state before external calls, rely on modern Solidity arithmetic safety, and enforce access and logging consistently.

Secure Smart Contract Development Practices
Design, code, and log defensively to reduce attack surface and operational risk.
Orientation

We cover the Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern, integer safety using Solidity 0.8.0, access control patterns, safe external calls, gas-aware design, and consistent event logging.

In this lesson

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will be able to apply concrete, repeatable coding practices that reduce the risk of critical smart contract failures. First, you will use the Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern as a default for any function making external calls so reentrancy becomes structurally unlikely. Second, you will rely on modern Solidity arithmetic safety or, for legacy code, SafeMath, so integer overflows and underflows fail fast rather than silently corrupting balances. Third, you will implement clear, reusable access checks with modifiers and role-based patterns so administrative functions cannot be called by unauthorized accounts. Fourth, you will handle external calls safely by checking the boolean success return, preferring call semantics that match your intent, and avoiding constructs that hide failure modes. Each objective is tied to a small coding habit that you can add to your pull-request checklist. For example, after this chapter you should be able to open a withdraw function and point to the checks, the state change, and the external call, and explain why that order matters. These skills make contracts easier to audit and maintain, and they reduce the chance of catastrophic post-deployment fixes.

keyIdea.text: Adopt CEI, arithmetic safety, modular access control, and careful external-call handling as everyday practices.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice & Quality
screens.subtitle: Habits that make your smart contracts maintainable and auditable

narration.text: This second objectives slide focuses on code hygiene and operational resilience. You will adopt patterns that make contracts easier to audit and less likely to fail under real conditions. First, you will design functions to avoid unbounded loops and large monolithic processing that can lead to denial-of-service or prohibitively expensive transactions. Second, you will add events for critical actions so off-chain systems can monitor, alert, and reconstruct state transitions during post-incident analysis. Third, you will structure refactors to prioritize readable modifiers and emit events after successful state changes so logs accurately reflect on-chain state. Fourth, you will practice checking external call success booleans and avoiding assumptions about gas forwarded by transfer or send. As a concrete example, when refactoring a vulnerable withdraw function, you will update balances first, use call and check its return value, and then emit a Withdrawal event. These habits improve both security and operability and are the difference between a contract that is hard to debug and one you can safely run in production.

screens.title: Checks-Effects-Interactions (CEI) Pattern
screens.subtitle: A simple ordering rule that prevents reentrancy and preserves state integrity

narration.text: The Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern is a simple but powerful rule: validate inputs and permissions first, then modify contract state, and finally make any external calls. The key idea is to avoid leaving critical state in a stale form when control passes to external code. A concrete example is a withdrawal function that first requires the user has sufficient balance, then reduces their balance and total staked amount, and finally performs the external transfer. This ordering prevents a malicious recipient from re-entering the withdrawal function and triggering another transfer before the contract's record was updated. A common misconception is that reentrancy is only about calls to well-known functions; in practice, any external call transfers control and can invoke fallback or receive code. Another subtle point: CEI is a mental default, but sometimes you also combine it with reentrancy guards for layered protection. For learners, practice by reading each function and asking: where are the checks, where are the effects, and do I call externally afterwards? If any external call appears before state updates, refactor the function to follow CEI. The core takeaway is to make correct state the smallest attack surface by committing changes before handing control out.

keyIdea.title: CEI Pattern
keyIdea.text: Always: perform checks, update state, then interact externally; this ordering prevents reentrancy exploiting stale state.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Checks-Effects-Interactions
Definition
CEI prescribes the order: checks, effects, interactions. Follow it for functions that perform external calls.
Pattern Steps
  1. Checks: validate inputs and permissions with require statements.
  2. Effects: update balances and contract state variables.
  3. Interactions: perform external calls, transfers, or calls to other contracts.
Concrete Example
A withdraw function that reduces the sender's balance before calling out ensures the sender cannot re-enter and withdraw twice.
Common mistake
Sending Ether before updating balances allows a recipient contract to call back into the original function and exploit stale state.
Annotated Code Walkthrough
// Secure against reentrancy using CEI
function withdrawSecure(uint _amount) public {
    // 1. Checks: Verify conditions
    require(stakedBalances[msg.sender] >= _amount, "Insufficient staked balance");

    // 2. Effects: Update state BEFORE external call
    stakedBalances[msg.sender] -= _amount;
    totalStaked -= _amount;

    // 3. Interactions: Perform external call
    (bool success, ) = msg.sender.call{value: _amount}("");
    require(success, "Withdrawal failed");
}
Key Takeaway
Order matters. Update state before calling others to avoid reentrancy.
Try this
Scan a withdraw function in a repo and mark where CEI is violated. Refactor to reorder steps.

screens.title: Integer Safety: Solidity 0.8.0 and SafeMath
screens.subtitle: Why overflow checks matter and how to get them

narration.text: Integer overflow and underflow used to be a frequent source of critical vulnerabilities. The essential risk is that arithmetic wraps silently: adding one to the maximum value can make it zero, and subtracting more than a balance can wrap to a huge number. Modern Solidity versions starting at 0.8.0 change the default: arithmetic operations now revert on overflow and underflow, which means the contract will fail loudly rather than produce corrupted values. For older contracts that still use an earlier compiler, libraries such as SafeMath were used to enforce checks explicitly by wrapping add, sub, mul, and div operations. A concrete example: when refactoring a token transfer on Solidity 0.7, you must replace plain additions and subtractions with SafeMath calls. When upgrading to 0.8.0, you can rely on built-in checks but still audit places where unchecked blocks are used. A common misconception is that SafeMath is always required; in modern code it is less necessary but still meaningful when reading or maintaining legacy code. The practical habit is to know the compiler version, inspect arithmetic, and write tests that attempt boundary cases to ensure operations revert as expected. This reduces surprising balance corruption and aligns behavior with developer intent.

keyIdea.title: Integer Safety
keyIdea.text: Use Solidity 0.8.0+ for automatic reverts on overflow; use SafeMath when maintaining older code to prevent silent wrapping.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Integer Safety
Comparison
Solidity 0.8.0+ reverts on overflow/underflow; legacy code used SafeMath to enforce safe arithmetic.
When to use which
  • New projects: compile with 0.8.0+ and rely on default checks.
  • Legacy code: keep SafeMath wrappers or upgrade carefully, testing edge cases.
  • Unchecked blocks: only use when you fully control inputs and need gas savings.
Concrete Task
Run unit tests that push values to maximum uint boundaries and assert operations revert as expected.
Code Example
// For legacy code (pre-0.8.0) using SafeMath
using SafeMath for uint;

function transfer(address to, uint amount) public {
    balances[msg.sender] = balances[msg.sender].sub(amount);
    balances[to] = balances[to].add(amount);
}

// Modern Solidity 0.8.0+ reverts automatically on overflow
function transferModern(address to, uint amount) public {
    require(balances[msg.sender] >= amount, "Insufficient balance");
    balances[msg.sender] -= amount; // safe in 0.8.0+
    balances[to] += amount;
}
Key Takeaway
Know your compiler version; test boundary arithmetic for safety.
Misconception
Assuming SafeMath is redundant without verifying compiler and unchecked sections can leave gaps.

screens.title: Robust Access Control: Modifiers and onlyOwner
screens.subtitle: Encapsulate permission checks to prevent accidental privilege leaks

narration.text: Access control is about making sure only authorized accounts can perform sensitive operations. A straightforward way to enforce this in Solidity is with modifiers and an explicit owner variable. Modifiers let you encapsulate checks like verifying that the caller is the contract owner, then apply that modifier to many functions, which reduces duplicated require statements and makes intent clear. For example, an onlyOwner modifier checks that the message sender equals the stored owner and then executes the function body. Use require to provide clear revert messages. For more complex permissioning, role-based access control associates named roles with addresses, allowing multiple administrators, minters, or pausers. A common mistake is assuming only private functions or comments will prevent misuse; on-chain enforcement must be explicit. Another pitfall is forgetting to protect ownership transfer paths and allowing a zero address to become the owner. As a concrete practice, when adding a setter like setTotalSupply, always apply an onlyOwner modifier and emit an event when ownership or important config changes. This habit reduces accidental misconfiguration and supports auditing of admin actions. Robust Access Control: Modifiers and onlyOwner means use modifiers for repeated checks, validate ownership in each privileged path, and emit events on administrative changes.. In practical terms, encapsulate permission checks to prevent accidental privilege leaks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Access Control
keyIdea.text: Use modifiers for repeated checks, validate ownership in each privileged path, and emit events on administrative changes.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Access Control
Why modifiers?
Modifiers centralize checks and improve readability; they make permission logic easy to audit across functions.
Example modifier
Declare an owner, initialize it in the constructor, and use onlyOwner to guard setters and administrative functions.
address public owner;

constructor(){
  owner = msg.sender;
}

modifier onlyOwner(){
  require(msg.sender == owner, "Only owner can call");
  _;
}

function transferOwnership(address _newOwner) public onlyOwner{
  require(_newOwner != address(0), "New owner cannot be zero address");
  owner = _newOwner;
}
Common pitfall
Leaving a public setter without a modifier or forgetting to check for zero addresses can open admin paths to attackers.
Role-Based Access Control
For complex systems, assign roles to addresses and check those roles rather than a single owner to enable fine-grained permissions.
Concrete practice
Use modifiers for common checks, add unit tests that assert only authorized accounts can call privileged functions, and emit events for ownership and role changes.
Key Takeaway
Explicit, testable access control prevents accidental privilege leaks and simplifies audits.
Try this
Add an onlyOwner modifier to a public setter and write a unit test that fails for non-owner callers.

screens.title: External Calls: call vs transfer/send
screens.subtitle: Understand gas implications and why you must check success booleans

narration.text: External calls are a point of control transfer and unpredictability. Historically, transfer and send forwarded a small, fixed amount of gas to the recipient, which protected contracts from reentrancy in certain cases but also caused unexpected failures when recipient fallback logic needed more gas. The recommendation in modern Solidity is to use call, which forwards all available gas by default and returns a boolean success value that you must check. This approach is safer when you intentionally want the recipient to run complex logic, but it requires you to write your code defensively: update state first, check the success boolean, and handle failures explicitly. A common misconception is that call is unsafe by default; call is simply more explicit and powerful, and its safety depends on how you order checks and effects around it. In practice, prefer call with a require on success, avoid assuming transfer will succeed, and write tests that simulate failing external calls. For functions that must be robust, also consider alternative patterns like pull payments, where recipients claim funds rather than the contract pushing funds to arbitrary addresses.

keyIdea.title: External call safety
keyIdea.text: Prefer call with success checks; avoid trusting transfer/send gas semantics and design push vs pull payment strategies deliberately.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › External Calls
Call Semantics Comparison
transfer / send
Forward limited gas (2300). Can fail if recipient logic needs more gas; historically used to limit reentrancy surface.
call
Forwards all available gas and returns (bool, data). Must check the boolean and handle failure paths explicitly.
Practical guideline
Use call with a require(success) after updating state, or use pull patterns to avoid complex push logic.
Concrete Example
(bool success, ) = recipient.call{value: amount}("");
require(success, "Transfer failed");

// Prefer this after state is updated to follow CEI
Key Takeaway
Checking call success is non-negotiable; design push vs pull carefully.
Misconception
Assuming transfer always succeeds hides cases where recipient fallback requires more gas.

screens.title: Gas Limits & DoS Prevention
screens.subtitle: Design to avoid operations that become too expensive to execute

narration.text: Gas constraints are an operational security consideration. When a function requires iterating over a collection that can grow without bound, it risks becoming uncallable because the gas cost will exceed block gas limits. This becomes a denial-of-service vector: either the contract can no longer process that action, or a malicious user forces the collection to grow so legitimate users cannot complete transactions. Practical solutions include pagination, processing in slices, or a pull-based pattern where users claim items individually. When designing token distributions or reward claims, prefer looping over bounded arrays with clear limits, or allow users to claim their slice rather than a single function trying to handle everyone. Another approach is to store pointers or cursors and let an off-chain caller complete the work in multiple transactions. A common misconception is thinking gas limits are purely a performance issue; they are a security surface because attackers can intentionally force gas-heavy states. A recommended habit is to estimate worst-case gas for each function and write tests that emulate large collections to ensure functions remain callable. Consider also refund and reentrancy interactions when designing multi-step processes, and prefer idempotent, resumable operations.

keyIdea.title: Gas-aware design
keyIdea.text: Avoid unbounded on-chain loops; prefer pagination, pull patterns, and resumable processes to prevent DoS by gas exhaustion.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Gas Limits & DoS
Problem
Unbounded loops or unbounded storage growth can make functions impossible to execute, opening a DoS vector.
Mitigation patterns
  • Paginate long lists and process in pages.
  • Use pull payments so users claim values individually.
  • Limit per-transaction work and use cursors for resumable processing.
Developer habit
Estimate worst-case gas, add tests simulating large datasets, and design operations to be incremental.
Concrete Example
Instead of a single function that distributes rewards to every account in a growing array, let each account call claimReward. Store each user's entitlement and mark claimed. If you must batch, process a fixed maximum number per transaction and track progress with an index.
Key Takeaway
Design operations so they are bounded and resumable to avoid gas-related DoS.
Try this
Take a function that iterates over an array and refactor it into a paginated processor with an index pointer and max batch size.

screens.title: Event Logging for Security and Observability
screens.subtitle: Emit clear events for critical state changes and administrative actions

narration.text: Events are how on-chain actions become visible to off-chain systems. Emitting well-structured events for withdrawals, configuration changes, and ownership transfers gives you an immutable audit trail that is invaluable for monitoring, debugging, and post-incident analysis. Events are cheap compared to storage and are the canonical way for wallets, explorers, and indexers to reconstruct what happened. A concrete practice is to emit a Withdrawal event with the user address and amount after a successful withdrawal, or emit ConfigUpdated when an admin changes a parameter. One misconception is that events are optional because state already records changes; in reality, events provide a timeline that is easier and lower-cost for off-chain auditing. Another misconception is emitting events before state updates: always emit after successful state changes so logs match on-chain state. Tests should include checks that events are emitted and contain the expected indexed fields. Finally, well-chosen indexing in events helps efficient filtering for monitors and incident response tools. Event Logging for Security and Observability means emit events after successful state changes to provide an auditable, low-cost trail for monitoring and debugging.. In practical terms, emit clear events for critical state changes and administrative actions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Events matter
keyIdea.text: Emit events after successful state changes to provide an auditable, low-cost trail for monitoring and debugging.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Event Logging
Why events?
Events are an append-only audit trail used by off-chain services to monitor contract behavior and reconstruct actions without reading internal storage directly.
Good event practices
  • Emit after state changes to keep logs consistent.
  • Index frequently-filtered fields like user addresses.
  • Include meaningful payloads to aid debugging.
Example events
event Withdrawal(address indexed user, uint amount);
event ConfigUpdated(address indexed setter, uint newValue);

// Emit after successful operations
emit Withdrawal(msg.sender, _amount);
emit ConfigUpdated(msg.sender, _value);
Key Takeaway
Events are essential for monitoring and post-incident analysis; emit them consistently.
Try this
Add event assertions to your unit tests so a successful action also verifies the emitted event contents.

screens.title: Refactoring VulnerableToken to SecureToken — Plan
screens.subtitle: A step-by-step checklist for the hands-on refactor

narration.text: Refactoring a vulnerable contract requires a clear checklist. Start by upgrading the compiler pragma to Solidity 0.8.0 or later to gain built-in arithmetic safety. Next, audit every arithmetic operation and remove or adapt SafeMath usage if upgrading, or add SafeMath calls for legacy code. Then add explicit access control: declare an owner, initialize it in the constructor, and implement an onlyOwner modifier. Apply this modifier to functions that change critical configuration such as total supply. For withdrawal and transfer functions, apply the CEI pattern: perform require checks, update balances, and only then perform external calls with call and a checked success value. Add events for transfers, withdrawals, and configuration changes and emit them after the state updates succeed. Finally, add unit tests for boundary arithmetic cases, ownership checks, and reentrancy scenarios. A common mistake is deploying incremental changes without tests; always run tests simulating failing external calls and large datasets. This checklist captures the chapter's practices and gives you a repeatable refactor flow. Refactoring VulnerableToken to SecureToken — Plan means upgrade compiler, enforce integer safety, centralize access control, apply cei, check external calls, emit events, and add tests.. In practical terms, a step-by-step checklist for the hands-on refactor. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Refactor checklist
keyIdea.text: Upgrade compiler, enforce integer safety, centralize access control, apply CEI, check external calls, emit events, and add tests.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Refactor Plan
Refactor checklist for SecureToken
1. Upgrade Compiler
Change pragma to ^0.8.0 to get automatic arithmetic checks and re-audit code.
2. Integer Safety
Remove unsafe arithmetic or replace with SafeMath if not upgrading; add boundary tests.
3. Add Owner & Modifiers
Implement onlyOwner and apply to setters like setTotalSupply.
4. Apply CEI
Ensure withdraw and transfer functions update state before external calls.
5. Check External Calls
Use call and assert the returned success boolean rather than assuming transfers succeed.
6. Emit Events & Tests
Emit Withdrawal and ConfigUpdated events and add tests for reentrancy, ownership, and arithmetic edges.
Concrete next step
Start by changing the pragma, run the compiler, and fix all arithmetic warnings. Then add onlyOwner and tests that fail for non-owners.

screens.subtitle: Guided walkthrough of the key code changes from VulnerableToken

screens.title: Pull Payments and Payment Design
screens.subtitle: Reduce risk by letting recipients claim funds instead of the contract pushing them

narration.text: Push payments where the contract iterates and sends funds to many recipients in one transaction are fragile. Pull payments invert the flow: the contract credits balances and users claim their funds in separate transactions. This avoids gas spikes, simplifies failure handling, and reduces the risk of a single transaction failing due to a slow or gas-hungry recipient. A concrete implementation stores owed amounts in a mapping and provides a claim function that follows CEI and a safe external call. Pull designs also make it easier to retry failed transfers because a failed claim does not block other users. A common misconception is that pull payments increase work for recipients; while they do require an extra transaction, they dramatically improve contract resilience and user control. When designing payments, combine pull patterns with event logging so off-chain services can notify users of available funds. Also consider gas limits for claim functions and encourage batch claims with bounded pagination if necessary. The architectural trade-off favors reliability and auditability over a single all-at-once distribution. Pull Payments and Payment Design means favor pull over push for distributions: credit balances and let recipients claim, which improves reliability and reduces gas-related failures.. In practical terms, reduce risk by letting recipients claim funds instead of the contract pushing them. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Pull payments
keyIdea.text: Favor pull over push for distributions: credit balances and let recipients claim, which improves reliability and reduces gas-related failures.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.3 › Pull Payments
Pattern Overview
Credit recipients in a mapping and provide a claim function so each recipient pulls their funds when ready.
Benefits
  • Avoids unbounded loops and gas spikes.
  • Makes retries and partial failures manageable.
  • Aligns with CEI when claims update state before calls.
Example Implementation
mapping(address => uint) public owed;

default function credit(address user, uint amount) internal {
  owed[user] += amount;
  emit Credited(user, amount);
}

function claim() public {
  uint amount = owed[msg.sender];
  require(amount > 0, "Nothing to claim");
  owed[msg.sender] = 0; // Effect before interaction
  (bool success, ) = msg.sender.call{value: amount}("");
  require(success, "Claim failed");
  emit Withdrawal(msg.sender, amount);
}
Key Takeaway
Pull payments increase reliability and align with CEI by isolating interactions per user.
Try this
Refactor a batched payout into a credit/claim flow and test with failing recipient mocks.

screens.title: Testing and Auditing Secure Contracts
screens.subtitle: Unit tests and scenario tests that prove the contract resists common failures

narration.text: Secure coding is only effective when backed by tests that validate behavior under edge conditions. Unit tests should cover arithmetic boundary cases, access control enforcement, and correct event emission. Scenario tests should simulate failing external calls, reentrancy attempts, and large data sets to ensure gas limits are respected. For CEI, write a test that deploys a malicious contract that attempts to re-enter a withdraw function; the refactored CEI-based withdraw should prevent repeated withdrawals. For integer safety, write tests that push values to maximum uint and assert operations revert. For access control, assert that non-owner transactions revert and that ownership transfer emits the right event and updates the owner variable. Automated tests combined with static analysis tools and manual code review provide layered assurance. narration.text: Let's consolidate the most important ideas. First, the Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern gives you a simple ordering rule that prevents many reentrancy issues: validate inputs, commit state changes, and then interact with external addresses. Second, integer safety is non-negotiable: modern Solidity reverts on overflows in 0.8.0 and later, but when working with older codebases use SafeMath and add boundary tests. Third, modifiers and role-based access control reduce duplication and make permission checks explicit and auditable. Each of these concepts is actionable: use CEI as a default for external calls, verify your compiler and arithmetic assumptions, and codify permissions with modifiers or standard RBAC libraries. These three form a minimal defensive baseline you should apply to most contracts before considering more advanced protections. narration.text: A few additional ideas complete the chapter's security picture. First, always check the success boolean returned by external calls and avoid trusting transfer/send gas semantics. Second, design for gas by avoiding unbounded loops and using pagination or pull payments for distributions. Third, emit well-structured events for key state changes so on-chain actions are observable and auditable by off-chain systems. Together these practices improve reliability, monitoring, and incident response. As a reflective question: when you next write a function that sends value or iterates over users, ask whether it follows CEI, whether payments should be pull-based, and whether you have tests that simulate failure modes. These quick checks will make your contracts significantly more resilient in production.
